newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Little to fear from G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Little to fear from G7 summit.

text.p: As global currency markets brace themselves for the outcome of this weekend's G7 meeting, bond markets are adopting a more laid back view and will take any repercussions in their stride, analysts said on Friday.

But on balance, with little expected in the way of a concerted effort to rein in the dollar's recent rise, they said U.S. Treasuries would likely be a better bet than Japanese government bonds for now.
"I think the G7, in terms of bonds, isn't going to have an enormous impact," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking. "So I would stay in the dollar bloc."
Finance ministers and central bank governors of the Group of Seven industrial nations -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada -- meet in Berlin on Saturday.
Top officials have made clear last month's surge of some six percent in the dollar against the mark and yen will be high on the agenda at the meeting.

But analysts expected governments to stop short of action to stem the yen's slide, and to issue a bland statement instead simply supporting a stable dollar or welcoming its normalisation from all-time lows.
"I don't expect any major agreements to come out of the G7," said Yamaichi International bond strategist Adam Chester.
"If that is the case, you could find the yen is sold off further...which from the JGB point of view would be negative. But there would be no great implications for U.S. Treasuries."

But Chester suggested keeping a wary eye on the U.S. bond market in the coming weeks, in case the Bank of Japan, frustrated by the lack of international support for the sagging yen, takes matters into its own hands and begins selling its vast stash of Treasury bonds.

"If there is no areement and the Bank of Japan decides to do something on its own, it could start selling U.S. Treasuries," said Chester. "Then the market could come under some pressure as the BoJ holds a significant amount of T-bonds."
Chester said the Japanese central bank holds around $217 billion of foreign exchange reserves, about $180 billion of which is estimated to be in U.S. Treasuries.
"So it could do some damage if it decides to take matters into its own hands," he said.
But any impact from the weekend's global gathering of financial bigwigs will be superseded in bond markets by more mundane domestic matters.
"The strong dollar does help to contain inflation and provides some support for bonds, but the key (for U.S. Treasuries) is domestic factors," said DKB International economist Nick Stamenkovic.
"As long as the market fears stronger growth, higher inflation and Fed tightening, Treasury market sentiment will continue to be negative."

Lewis agreed that Friday's January payrolls data held greater significance for U.S. Treasuries. "The labour report is far more important for bonds than the G7 -- from that point of view I wouldn't be holding Treasuries," he said.

The flip side of any continued rise in the dollar after the absence of a strongly-worded post G7 communique, will likely be ongoing support for European high yielders as the German mark continues to suffer, analysts said. "Whatever U.S. Treasuries do in response to the G7, European markets will be affected," said Chester.
"It'll have a good knock-on effect on high yielders if the dollar continues to strengthen."
